what_its_for: Ecallantide is used to treat sudden attacks of hereditary angioedema (HAE) in adults and children 12 years and older. HAE causes sudden, severe swelling in different parts of the body such as the hands, feet, face, throat, stomach, and genitals. This medicine works by blocking a protein in your body that causes this swelling.
how_to_take: Ecallantide is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in the stomach area, thigh, or upper arm. It must be given by a trained healthcare provider in a medical setting because of the risk of serious allergic reactions. You should NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Three separate injections are given one after another during each treatment session.
dosing: The usual dose is 30 mg total, given as three separate injections of 10 mg each (1 mL per injection) into different areas of the skin. All three injections are given during the same HAE attack episode. If your symptoms come back or do not improve, your doctor may give you another 30 mg dose within 24 hours.
missed_dose: Because ecallantide is only given during an acute HAE attack in a medical setting, a traditional missed dose schedule does not apply. If you experience an HAE attack, contact your healthcare provider or go to a medical facility right away so you can receive treatment as soon as possible.
storage: Ecallantide should be stored in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it. If taken out of the refrigerator, it can be kept at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 14 days, but it must be used or thrown away within that time. Do not use it if it looks cloudy, has particles in it, or if the expiration date has passed.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you have ever had an allergic reaction to ecallantide before, as you should not receive it again if you have. Avoid delaying treatment during an HAE attack — swelling in the throat can be life-threatening. Do not attempt to inject this medicine yourself at home without proper medical training and supervision.
when_to_call_doctor: Seek emergency medical help immediately if you experience any signs of a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) after receiving this medicine. Warning signs include: sudden rash, hives, or itching; swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; difficulty breathing or wheezing; chest tightness; dizziness, fainting, or a fast heartbeat; nausea or vomiting right after the injection. Also call your doctor if your HAE symptoms do not improve after treatment or if swelling gets worse, especially in the throat or airway.
when_it_works: Ecallantide begins to work relatively quickly after injection. Many patients start to notice some improvement in their HAE symptoms within 4 hours of receiving the injections. The medicine works by blocking kallikrein, a protein that triggers swelling during an HAE attack, helping to reduce swelling and relieve pain and discomfort.
special_populations: Children under 12 years old: Ecallantide is not approved for use in children younger than 12. Pregnancy: It is not fully known if ecallantide is safe during pregnancy. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is unknown if ecallantide passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Elderly patients: Ecallantide has not been studied extensively in older adults, but no specific dose adjustments are currently recommended. Always inform your healthcare provider of all your medical conditions and medications before receiving this treatment.
